headline: Free Video App VLC Hits 7 Billion Downloads

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: VLC is a video player that people can download for free on their computers, phones, and tablets. It lets you watch movies and videos without needing the internet, unlike many streaming apps that cost money every month. A group called VideoLAN makes VLC, and they do not charge people to use it. Recently, VLC reached a huge number: 7 billion downloads! That means people all around the world have downloaded it 7 billion times. Just a year and a half ago, VLC had only reached 6 billion downloads, so it is growing fast. The people who make VLC are also working to make it work on more devices, like new smart TVs made by Amazon. They are also building a brand new version called VLC 4, though it is taking a while to finish. VLC's success shows that free, helpful tools can be just as popular as expensive ones. Many people like VLC because it works almost everywhere and does not cost anything.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: VLC is a well-known video and media player that anyone can download for free. It is made by a non-profit group called VideoLAN, which means the company is not trying to make money like most streaming services such as Netflix or Disney+. Instead, VideoLAN offers VLC completely free and lets people watch videos without needing an internet connection. Recently, VLC crossed a major milestone of 7 billion total downloads across every kind of device, including phones, computers, and tablets. This is a fast jump, since VLC had only hit 6 billion downloads about eighteen months earlier. The people behind VLC keep expanding where it works. They just added support for Amazon's new Vega operating system, which is used for smart TVs, so people can now watch VLC content there too. VLC's team is also creating a big update called VLC 4, though it is taking longer than expected to finish. Last year, they hinted at adding artificial intelligence tools that could translate videos and create subtitles automatically, using computer programs that run directly on your device instead of the internet. It's unclear if that feature has been released yet. VLC's huge popularity shows that people appreciate free, flexible software that works on almost any device, especially compared to paid streaming platforms that can be expensive and limited to certain devices.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: In a time when most video streaming services charge monthly fees, VLC stands out because it is completely free and works offline. Made by VideoLAN, a non-profit organization, VLC has just reached an impressive milestone: 7 billion downloads worldwide across every type of device. This growth has been rapid — VLC only reached 6 billion downloads about a year and a half ago, meaning it gained a billion more downloads in a relatively short amount of time. Jean-Baptiste Kempf, the president and lead developer of VLC, shared this update, along with news about the software's ongoing development. VideoLAN recently made VLC available on Amazon's new Vega operating system, which is used to run smart TVs. This means people can now use VLC on more devices than before, expanding its reach even further. The team is also working on supporting more video and audio formats, known as codecs, which are the different ways video and sound files are compressed and played back. Additionally, VideoLAN is developing a major new update called VLC 4, though the release has taken longer than expected. Last year, the company also mentioned plans for AI-powered features, including automatic translation and subtitle generation that would work using local computer programs rather than needing an internet connection. However, it's unclear whether these AI features were ever actually released to users. VLC's continued growth and popularity highlight something important: many people value free, flexible technology that isn't locked behind paywalls or limited to specific devices. As streaming subscriptions become more expensive and complicated, with content spread across many different paid services, VLC offers a simple, no-cost alternative that just works. Its non-profit structure also means the software isn't designed to make a profit or push ads, which makes it appealing to users who want a straightforward media player without commercial interruptions.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: VLC media player, one of the most widely used pieces of free software in the world, has just crossed a remarkable milestone of 7 billion total downloads across all platforms. This achievement comes from VideoLAN, a non-profit organization that has committed to keeping VLC free and open for anyone to use, in contrast to the many paid subscription-based streaming platforms that dominate the entertainment industry today. Jean-Baptiste Kempf, VLC's president and lead developer, announced the news, noting that the app had only reached 6 billion downloads about eighteen months earlier, in January of the previous year. This rapid growth from 6 billion to 7 billion downloads in such a short time shows just how widely VLC continues to be adopted, even as streaming services expand and multiply. Part of VLC's ongoing appeal lies in its flexibility. The software works offline, meaning users don't need an internet connection to watch downloaded videos, and it supports a huge variety of file formats and codecs, which are the technical methods used to compress and play back video and audio. This adaptability makes VLC useful in situations where other apps might fail, such as playing an unusual video file format that a paid streaming app wouldn't support. VideoLAN continues to expand VLC's reach, recently porting the software to Amazon's new Vega operating system, which powers certain smart TVs. This kind of expansion ensures VLC remains accessible even as new devices and operating systems emerge in the market. Additionally, the company is developing VLC 4, a major new update, though its release has been delayed as development continues. Last year, VideoLAN also revealed plans to bring AI-powered translation and subtitle tools to the platform, with the unique feature of running these AI models locally on a user's device rather than relying on cloud-based services. This would mean users could get automatic subtitles or translations without needing an internet connection or sending their data to outside servers, which raises fewer privacy concerns compared to cloud-based AI tools. However, it remains unclear whether these features have been fully released. VLC's continued success reflects a larger conversation about digital access and affordability, as free, open-source software increasingly competes with costly subscription models in the world of streaming and media consumption.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: VLC media player, developed by the non-profit organization VideoLAN, has surpassed 7 billion downloads across all platforms, marking a significant milestone in the world of free, open-source software. This announcement, shared by VLC's president and lead developer Jean-Baptiste Kempf, highlights not just the software's popularity but the broader appeal of free alternatives in an industry increasingly dominated by paid subscription services. Notably, VLC reached 6 billion downloads only about eighteen months earlier, in January of the prior year, meaning the app gained roughly a billion new downloads in a relatively compressed timeframe — a testament to its sustained relevance nearly three decades after its initial release. Unlike commercial streaming platforms such as Netflix or Disney+, which require ongoing payment and often restrict content based on licensing agreements or geographic region, VLC operates as a free, offline-capable media player that can play nearly any video or audio file format. This versatility stems from its extensive support for various codecs — the technical standards used to compress and decompress video and audio data — which allows VLC to play files that many other media players cannot handle. Because VideoLAN operates as a non-profit, its priority is not shareholder profit but rather maintaining accessible, functional software for as many users and devices as possible. This model has allowed VLC to remain free of advertisements and paywalls, a rarity in today's digital media landscape. VideoLAN continues to expand the software's compatibility, having recently completed a port to Amazon's new Vega operating system, which is used to power certain smart televisions. This expansion reflects an ongoing effort to keep VLC relevant as the technology landscape shifts toward new operating systems and device ecosystems. Additionally, the organization is actively developing VLC 4, a major overhaul of the software, though its release has faced repeated delays as the development team works through the complexities of a large-scale update. Last year, VideoLAN also teased upcoming features involving artificial intelligence, specifically automatic translation and subtitle generation powered by locally-run AI models rather than cloud-based services. This distinction matters: local AI processing would allow users to generate subtitles or translations without transmitting data over the internet, offering greater privacy and functioning even without an internet connection. However, it remains unclear whether these AI features have been implemented in current releases of the software. VLC's continued growth underscores a broader tension in the digital media world between the increasing cost and fragmentation of streaming services and the enduring demand for accessible, universally compatible, and privacy-respecting alternatives. As more entertainment content becomes locked behind subscription paywalls, tools like VLC demonstrate that free and open-source software can still thrive and expand its user base substantially.

questions: Why do you think a free tool like VLC has been downloaded so many times, even though there are many paid streaming services available?
How might having software that works on almost any device, without needing the internet, be helpful in your own life or in your school?
What do you think are the benefits and possible downsides of software being made by a non-profit group instead of a company trying to earn money?
